content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a comprehensive handbook in 2014 to guide the development of health-related guidelines, emphasizing evidence-based practices. 2. A meta-analysis conducted by Kröll, Doebler, and Nüesch in 2017 demonstrated the effectiveness of workplace stress management interventions in improving employee well-being and reducing stress. 3. Daniels and colleagues systematically reviewed intervention studies in 2017, highlighting the impact of job design and employment practices on employee well-being and organizational outcomes. 4. Verbeek and collaborators conducted a scoping review in 2019, focusing on interventions aimed at enhancing recovery among healthy workers, with findings published in Occupational Medicine. 5. Shrestha et al. (2018) reviewed workplace interventions designed to reduce sedentary behavior, emphasizing their potential to improve employee health outcomes. 6. Nagieh and colleagues (2015) systematically reviewed organizational interventions targeting teacher well-being and stress reduction, with findings published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 7. Joyce et al. (2010) explored the effects of flexible working conditions on employee health and well-being, providing evidence of their benefits in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 8. Lau and Mak (2017) conducted a meta-analysis on the effectiveness of workplace interventions for depression in Asia, revealing significant improvements in mental health outcomes. 9. Mlekus and Maier (2021) analyzed the impact of job and task rotation, concluding that its benefits may be overstated compared to its actual effectiveness. 10. Aronsson and colleagues (2017) systematically reviewed the relationship between work environments and burnout symptoms, identifying key factors contributing to employee mental health challenges. 11. Van der Molen et al. (2020) updated a systematic review and meta-analysis on work-related psychosocial risk factors for stress-related mental disorders, published in BMJ Open. 12. Rugulies and collaborators (2021) examined the effects of long working hours on depression, providing evidence through a systematic review and meta-analysis conducted under the WHO/ILO Joint Estimates initiative. 13. Virtanen et al. (2018) systematically reviewed the association between long working hours and depressive symptoms, incorporating both published studies and unpublished individual participant data. 14. Virtanen and colleagues (2015) also investigated the link between long working hours and alcohol use, presenting their findings in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in BMJ. 15. Richter et al. (2021) reviewed the literature on shift work and alcohol consumption, identifying significant associations between these factors and employee health outcomes. 16. Milner and collaborators (2018) conducted a meta-analysis on psychosocial job stressors and their relationship with suicidality, highlighting the importance of workplace mental health interventions. 17. Theorell et al. (2015) systematically reviewed the connection between work environments and depressive symptoms, emphasizing the role of organizational factors in mental health. 18. Duchaine and colleagues (2020) analyzed the impact of workplace psychosocial stressors on sickness absence due to diagnosed mental disorders, publishing their findings in JAMA Psychiatry. 19. Madsen et al. (2017) reviewed the role of job strain as a risk factor for clinical depression, incorporating individual participant data in their meta-analysis. 20. Verkuil, Atasayi, and Molendijk (2015) conducted a meta-analysis on workplace bullying and its effects on mental health, using both cross-sectional and longitudinal data. 21. Rudkjoebing et al. 22. Schmidt and colleagues (2014) examined the effects of role ambiguity and role conflict in the workplace, linking these factors to depression through a meta-analysis. 23. Kim and von dem Knesebeck (2015) reviewed the association between perceived job insecurity, unemployment, and depressive symptoms, focusing on prospective observational studies. 24. Milner et al. 25. Rugulies, Aust, and Madsen (2017) reviewed the impact of effort-reward imbalance at work on the risk of depressive disorders, emphasizing the importance of equitable workplace practices. 26. Yoshimura et al. (2013) conducted a cost-benefit analysis of primary prevention programs for mental health in Japanese workplaces, highlighting their economic and health benefits. 27. The International Labour Organization (ILO) has established global guidelines on decent work practices, emphasizing the importance of health protection in the workplace. 28. Houtman and colleagues, in collaboration with the WHO, provided advice to employers and worker representatives in developing countries on addressing workplace stress. 29. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, underscores the right to safe and healthy working conditions as a fundamental human right. 30. The WHO's global strategy on health, environment, and climate change outlines the transformative steps needed to improve lives and well-being through sustainable practices. 31. McCulloch, Rathbone, and Catchpole (2011) reviewed interventions aimed at improving teamwork and communication among healthcare staff, emphasizing their role in enhancing patient care. 32. Romppanen and Häggman-Laitila (2017) systematically reviewed interventions to improve nurses' well-being at work, identifying effective strategies for reducing stress and burnout. 33. Sakuraya et al. (2020) conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to determine the effectiveness of interventions in improving workers' subjective well-being. 34. Panagioti and colleagues (2017) reviewed controlled interventions to reduce burnout in physicians, providing evidence of their effectiveness in JAMA Internal Medicine. 35. The WHO's global strategy on human resources for health, Workforce 2030, emphasizes the importance of investing in health workforce development to achieve sustainable health outcomes.
